title: Writing 35th Street at Joe Garman's Paradise
summary: After the Entertainers Cafe the band moves to Garman's Paradise. Levy writes 35th Street, which Mayo Williams places for recording, and discusses its form.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

no. He really was a tough man. He had a tough lip and he could hit the high notes. He really could play. He was with Simon Stewart later. Yeah, he was with Simon Stewart later. And after we left the entertainers' cafe, we went to Joe Garman's Paradise there at Prairie and 35th. And that's when I wrote that 35th Street thing that they call the blues. Which isn't the blues. Oh, that's the 35th... It just says 35th Street, and I gave it to Mayo Williams. He was with Paramount Records. Mayo liked it, and he said, I'm going to give it to General Martin to record. I said, alright. I said, but why don't you get a vocalist? I said, because it's more of a vocal number than an instrumental. I said, because it tells all about 35th Street. I've been to Paris. I've seen Paris Boulevard again. I've been to all of Europe and everything. Gotta come back to 35th Street because it's the great white way up Chicago then. And later on, the Sunset Cafe, that was on 35th Street, and... Plantation? Plantation, yeah. That's when... Apex? Yeah. Apex was there. Earl Hines was playing Apex upstairs. 35th Street, that's why I wrote the number. And so, I guess the people in the Paramount Record Company told me, well, you know, I had to sell it, we better put blues on there, so... So the write-up. So when they got Riverside's album there, they criticized it was it wasn't the blues, but I started to write the fellow a letter and tell him, no, it wasn't the blues that I knew when I wrote
